source_text: OK, with the M-aif-over-the-operator plan, given that we now have an alignment with the WM phases, we can also think of *me* simulating the War Machine, just as we can think of it simulating me.  Obviously we go about things in different ways but since there is a phase-by-phase alignment I wonder if we can start to introduce the AIF formalism into the operator-facing work to develop some analytics.  Also, there are some points of interface, e.g., the machine is supposed to produce a Morning Brief which allows me to review..  In principle this allows me to "🈘" at the level of War Machine operations, though that is, for now, just an interesting observation, not necessarily the best place to start modelling my contributions.  However, the fact that I have been "donating" the learning functionality needed to build the War Machine is another interesting fact; some of that learning is reflected in the current plop-2026  paper as "Later reflection" sidenotes, but that collection of notes could probably be considerably refined by looking at records from the Evidence Landscape since the pinned 36d156218 paper version that we are annotating.

reply_text:
Three "Later reflection" notes so far. I'm now checking how much evidence has been recorded since the pinned paper version, so the proposal can rest on actual numbers.㊥ Gist: I'd start with two things, and both are cheap. The first is a descriptive count of your turns by AIF phase, built from 象's intent readings. The second is a sweep of the evidence recorded since the pinned paper (`36d1562`) for new "Later reflection" candidates. A proper generative model of you can come after those. Shall I add both to M-aif-over-the-operator as work items and send the sweep to codex-10, who wrote the margin-note injector?

㊟ (you simulating the War Machine) The phase alignment works in both directions, but the two directions have different amounts of data behind them. The mission's response model is the War Machine modelling you: it predicts whether you'll accept, decline or not answer an offer, and that prediction is its Q(o|π). For you modelling the machine, your observations would be the Morning Brief and the feed. Your 🈘 at the level of War Machine operations would then be your SELECT acting on the machine's policy. Very few records of that exchange exist yet, so I agree it's a poor place to start.

㭭 (analytics from the intent table) The legend already maps each intent to a phase, so the first analytic needs no new theory. For a window of your turns, count how many fall in each phase and which phase follows which. Then count your 🈚 disagree, 🈘 redirect and 🈹 retract turns as a share of the agent proposals they answer. That share is a rough measure of where the agents' predictions of you go wrong. Once those numbers exist, we can decide whether an AIF model of you would explain anything they don't.

㊢ (the "Later reflection" notes) There are currently three, in `p4ng/plop-2026-reflections.json`: R9 (the E-verdict facade, 2026-09-20), R16 (the selection-input backdoors, 09-30) and R17 (discharge-trained learning, 10-01). All three cite futon2 commits. The R17 note already describes what you call donating learning: implementation work now separates a pattern that was selected from one that was applied and from one that succeeded. That is the same distinction the response model needs for your corrections.

㊩ (sweeping the evidence) The volume is too large to read. Asking futon1b for everything since the pin returned 1,000 entries covering only the last three hours of today, and 843 of them were coordination traffic. A sweep needs filters. Three candidates:
- war-room cards (this turn came with wr-26);
- your corrections (🈚, 🈘 and 🈹 turns) together with the commits that followed them;
- commits whose messages name one of the paper's R-patterns.

Each candidate would fill the existing schema (pattern, date, repo, revisions, text), and you would pick which ones go into the margin.

🈸 (one decision) Shall I add these two items to the mission and dispatch the sweep? Reply `yes` to do both, or name just one.

previous_reply_acts.text: (where the icon came from) It's not on the 1984 sheets the other chips were cut from. On the Workshop panel in `CW_Coding_Screen.png`, the 4th icon on row 2 is the minus sign. I found it in the game's own icon file, `chipwits-native/data/IBOL` (160×160, 1-bit), in the bottom row. I cut it to the same 15-pixel black-on-transparent format as `chips/op-x-arrow.png`.
